Restingplace
REST-ing-plase
n. (a place of repose; the fold where a flock lies down)
Hebrew rebets, a place of lying down, from rabats, to crouch or lie down — used of flocks settling in a fold. The Authorized Version writes it as one word; the image throughout is pastoral.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

My people hath been lost sheep: their shepherds have caused them to go astray, they have turned them away on the mountains: they have gone from mountain to hill, they have forgotten their restingplace. The indictment falls on the shepherds first, and the sequence is precise. The sheep are lost, but they are lost because those set over them caused them to go astray. The wandering follows: from mountain to hill, a picture of restless movement with no fold at the end of it. And the final clause names the real loss — they have forgotten their restingplace. The Hebrew rebets is where a flock lies down, and lying down is the sign that a sheep feels safe; a flock that will not lie down is a flock that has no shepherd it trusts. This is the language of the twenty-third psalm from the far side: he maketh me to lie down in green pastures. Jeremiah adds the consequence in the next verse, that all who found them devoured them, and that their adversaries excused themselves by saying, We offend not, because they have sinned against the LORD, the habitation of justice. The remedy runs through the whole of Scripture in the same pastoral vocabulary, and the Lord speaks it directly: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Hebrews holds out the same thing as still future and still open: there remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), under RESTING-PLACE: a place for rest; a place where repose may be had.

expand to see more

RESTING-PLACE, n. A place for rest; a place where rest or repose may be obtained.

REST, n. Cessation of motion or action of any kind; quiet; repose; a state of quiet.

REST, n. Sleep; also, the final sleep; death; and hence, quiet, peace, or happiness in a future life.

FOLD, n. A pen or inclosure for sheep; a place where a flock of sheep is kept.

SHEPHERD, n. One who has the care of a flock; figuratively, a pastor, a minister of the gospel.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 50:6 — "My people hath been lost sheep: their shepherds have caused them to go astray, they have turned them away on the mountains: they have gone from mountain to hill, they have forgotten their restingplace."

Psalm 23:2 — "He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters."

Matthew 11:28 — "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."

Hebrews 4:9 — "There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God."

Modern Corruption

Rest is widely reduced to leisure or to the management of stress, and the responsibility of shepherds for a wandering flock is quietly dropped; Jeremiah assigns the blame first to the leaders.

expand to see more

The therapeutic account of rest treats it as recovery — time away, balance restored, stress managed — and there is a real creational goodness in sleep and sabbath that Scripture affirms without embarrassment. But the rest Jeremiah's sheep have forgotten is not a break from work. It is a place to lie down, and lying down in the pastoral image is what an animal does when it is not afraid. The Lord offers that to the labouring and heavy laden, and the offer terminates on himself: come unto me. A believer who has managed his schedule and not come to Christ has arranged his exhaustion more comfortably.

The verse is also a warning to those who teach, and it is not softened anywhere in Scripture. Their shepherds have caused them to go astray — the flock is lost, and the responsibility is assigned upward. Ezekiel devotes a chapter to the same charge, and James warns that teachers shall receive the greater condemnation. Where a congregation is restless, unfed, and moving from one thing to the next, the first question the Bible asks is not about the sheep. It is a hard word for ministers, and its hardness is exactly proportioned to the seriousness of the office.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew rebets (H7258), a place of lying down; rabats (H7257), to crouch, to lie down; roeh (H7462), a shepherd; taah (H8582), to wander or go astray.

expand to see more

Hebrew rebets (H7258) — a resting place, a fold where a flock lies down; rendered restingplace.

Hebrew rabats (H7257) — to lie down, to crouch; rendered maketh me to lie down at Psalm 23:2.

Hebrew roeh (H7462) — a shepherd, one who feeds; those charged with the straying.

Hebrew taah (H8582) — to wander, to go astray; the condition of the flock.

Greek sabbatismos (G4520) — a sabbath rest; there remaineth a rest to the people of God.

Usage

"“they have forgotten their restingplace” — the fold where a flock lies down."

"“their shepherds have caused them to go astray” — responsibility assigned."

"“I will give you rest” — the offer, terminating on Christ."
